title: Co-expression patterns explain how a basic transcriptional role for MYC modulates Wnt and MAPK pathways in colon and lung adenocarcinomas
author: Melanie Haas Kucherlapati
text:
ABSTRACT
A subset of proliferation genes that are associated with origin licensing, firing, and DNA synthesis has been compared to known drivers of colon (COAD) and lung (LUAD) adenocarcinomas using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients. The frequency with which APC, CTNNB1, KRAS, MYC, Braf, TP53, Rb1, EGFR, and cell cycle components have direct or indirect co-expression with the proliferation factors permits identification of their expression relative to the G1-S phase of the cell cycle. Here, adenomatous polyposis coli (APC), a negative regulator of Wnt signaling known to function through MYC, indirectly co-expresses at the same frequency as proliferation genes in both COAD and LUAD, consistent with M phase expression. However, APC is indirectly co-expressed with MYC and is found mutated only in COAD. MYC is thought to function at the interface of transcription and replication, acting through the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, and increased or decreased expression of MYC can induce or repress tumorigenesis, respectively. These data suggest that transcription of APC during the M phase with low MYC co-expression contributes by an unknown mechanism to APC mutations and Wnt pathway deregulation in COAD and that upper and lower limits of MYC expression, enforced by the cell cycle, may influence cancer differentially. Other Wnt signaling components co-expressed in the low MYC context in COAD also have significantly higher mutation frequencies, supporting the hypothesis. Additionally, Braf is found here to have direct co-expression with multiple proliferation factors in non-EGFR activated LUAD, and EGFR-activated LUAD are completely deregulated with respect to E2F(s) 4/5/6 expression, potentially explaining the low proliferation rates seen in LUAD.

Background
The adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) tumor suppressor gene is mutated in 70–80% of all colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) cases [1]. APC, expressed during M phase [2], controls proliferation through MYC, which is normally expressed in S phase [3]. The resulting dysregulation of the Wnt signaling pathway is facilitated by changes to the cytoskeleton regulated mostly by APC truncation mutation and CTNNB1 activation. A body of evidence also implicates the Wnt signaling pathway in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) development and progression. Model systems have shown that the pathway is essential for initiation and maintenance of Braf driven tumors [4,5]; KRAS and Braf tumor progression occurs with Wnt pathway activation [6]. Metastasis has been associated with increased Wnt expression [7,8]. However APC mutation happens with far less frequency in LUAD than it does in COAD [9,10].
Although proliferation of both COAD and LUAD involves deregulation of the Wnt signaling pathway, the canonical pathways taken by the two tumor types seem to be different. The aim of this study was to better understand how both Wnt and MAPK signaling pathways are modulated in these two tumor types. Spearman’s co-expression correlations have been used to examine the relationship of proliferation gene expression with the expression of selected cell cycle components and drivers involved in Wnt and MAPK signaling pathways. They have also been used to examine the relationship of MYC versus APC in different COAD and LUAD cohorts.
In addition to cell-specific therapeutics, identification of Wnt signaling modulation has relevance for immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy as its aberrant activation provides escape mechanisms [11]. While c-MYC effects various cellular processes, it also plays a role in host immunity and tumor microenvironment [12]. It has long been known to translocate into immunoglobulin switch regions in B cells in many cancers, including Burkitt’s lymphoma [13]. A body of evidence indicates that translocations are a result of R-loops targeted by activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), leading to double-stranded breaks and non-homologous end joining (NEHJ). Also seen in yeast THO mutants, the study underscores the importance of mRNP biogenesis in preventing genome instability through uracil incorporation into the DNA [14].
MYC regulates many genes [15,16] and currently is thought to function in basic transcription freeing promoters from stalled RNA polymerase complexes coordinating transcription elongation with cell cycle progression, preventing replication–transcription conflicts when “head-to-head” collisions occur between POLII and DNA polymerases, and restricting “R loop” formation (Figure 1) [14,17–21], roles which could explain how APC comes to be mutated in COAD but not in LUAD and have ramifications, with APC as a paradigm, for why it has been so difficult to find mutated drivers in some LUAD.
c-MYC knockout mice are embryonic lethal between 9.5 and 10.5 days of gestation; the gene can be completely removed from ES cells and the embryos before that time [22]. Homozygous lethality is not attributable to defects in a particular organ system, and animals are smaller and undernourished because of lower yolk sac circulation; heterozygotes have decreased fertility. Studies using Tet-regulatory transgenic mice demonstrated reversible tumorigenesis upon transgene-MYC inactivation [23,24]. MYC inactivation changes chromatin structure by reducing histone H4 acetylation and increasing histone H3 K9 methylation [25], increasing the transcriptionally inactive state of chromatin. Inactivation also causes cellular senescence through TP53 [25]. In the TCGA COAD cohort, many cases have APC mutated in the context of TP53 mutation, making senescence impossible and cellular immortality likely. Alternatively, as some COAD with APC mutation do not have TP53 mutation, it may be that MYC is not completely turned off at M phase in some cases, leading to persistent R loops causative of APC truncation.
LUAD has been separated in this study into “non-EGFR-” and “EGFR-activated” groups; other known pathways of tumorigenesis are not observed. EGFR-activated tumors (all non-treated) have relatively low proliferative capacity and appear to have stopped DNA synthesis as part of a DNA damage checkpoint [26] or as part of an embryonic diapause-like mechanism. In “EGFR-activated” cases, co-expression of the proliferative subset with E2Fs 1–8 shows that canonical repressor E2Fs 4/5/6 co-expression are completely unsynchronized.
Methods
Tumor cohorts
The colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) tumor cohort used throughout this study was assembled and analyzed by The Cancer Genome Atlas network (TCGA) [1]. COAD clusters were defined as having “Chromosomal Instability” (CIN), “Genome stabile” (GS), “Microsatellite unstable” (MMR), or “POLE “mutation. Lung adenocarcinomas (LUAD), also assembled and analyzed by TCGA [9,10], were placed into six clusters based on copy number, DNA methylation, and mRNA expression. Clusters for both COAD and LUAD were identified in heat maps for individual genes and their exons. All mutation, expression, and co-expression data generated by TCGA are available in cBioPortal [27–29], the Genome Data Commons [30], and the Broad Institute [31].
Proliferation genes examined
This study examines 31 proliferation genes known to be associated with origin licensing, firing, and DNA synthesis (Supplemental Table S1). These genes, subsequently referred to as the “subset”, are used as a marker of replication potential; selection was based on function and included a substantial number of genes viewed as essential to non-neoplastic replication initiation and processing. Test genes are compared to each gene of the subset and the frequency of significant comparisons reported.
By way of clarification, many processes (e.g. DNA damage response, repair mechanisms, mitosis) closely associated with proliferation are not being measured directly by the subset. The point of the exclusion was to make the comparisons as specific as possible to active DNA synthesis without pauses and non-neoplastic S phase.
Co-expression determination
Spearman’s correlation (rs) [32] is used to identify significant co-expression (mRNA, RNA Seq V2 RSEM) relationships identified as “direct”, “indirect”, or “none” found by the formula

rs (ρ) was calculated by cBioPortal [27], and significance was determined by two-sided t test with Benjamini Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction procedure applied. Spearman’s correlation coefficient can take values from +1 to −1, where +1 indicates perfect association, zero indicates no association, and −1 indicates a perfect negative association. Lack of co-expression (strength and direction) upon ranking is taken to indicate that the levels of gene product in question are not coordinated with origin licensing, firing, or “normal” DNA synthesis. This could occur under two conditions, either the genes never were transcriptionally coordinated or they lost regulation of expression due to tumorigenesis. Both the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) Database [33] and relevant literature are used to discriminate one possibility from the other. Observations suggested by co-expression were validated with other cBioPortal tools (e.g. expression heat maps) when necessary.
Other statistical tests
Fisher’s exact test was performed [34] to determine significance of proliferation factors with direct versus no direct association between COAD and LUAD, for cyclin regulator genes CCNH, CCNK, and CCNC and MYC.
An unpaired t-test/two-tailed test was performed [35] to determine significance in the means of C to T mutations, and APC/EGFR expression levels, between COAD and LUAD.
Chi-square analysis with Yates correction was performed [34] (as values are too large for Fisher’s exact) to determine significance of the number of mutations versus wild types in Wnt signaling genes (SMAD(s) 2–4, TCF7L2, APC, TP53, CSNK2A1, FZD1, and CCND1) in COAD versus LUAD PANCAN cases.
Results
Because of the complexity of cell cycling, Wnt, and KRAS signaling, in each segment of “Results”, a brief statement is given explaining the relevant gene’s normal function prior to describing the study’s findings.
APC, CTNNB1, MYC, and KRAS
APC is an antagonist of Wnt signaling [36–38]. MYC functions downstream of APC [3] and is involved in many biological processes and tumor types [24]. MYC and KRAS have been shown extensively to coordinate to influence proliferation and other processes [39].
In COAD, APC co-expression with the proliferation subset ranked “indirect” with high frequency; MYC and KRAS both ranked directly (Table 1). In LUAD, APC also co-expressed with the subset indirectly; MYC and KRAS direct co-expression was reduced. Deregulation was more pronounced in EGFR-activated LUAD over non-EGFR-activated LUAD.

CTNNB1 binds APC anchoring the actin cytoskeleton to regulate contact inhibition, additionally acting as a transcriptional activator with TCF/LEF p300/CBP of Wnt signaling. CTNNB1 did not co-express with the proliferation subset in either COAD or LUAD (Table 1). CTNNB1 did not have direct Spearman correlation with highly mutated APC in COAD, and it had significant direct correlation with predominantly non-mutated APC in LUAD (data not shown); these findings reflect its known function.
To explore why APC would have the potential to function as a tumor suppressor in LUAD but not sustain mutation, transcriptional levels, mutations, and mutational signature of the gene were examined between the two tumor types. In COAD, the most APC mutations are found in the last exon of the gene (exon 17) (Figure 2a-b), which codes for approximately 77% of the gene product. Transcriptional levels (RNA Seq V2 RSEM) of the APC gene were higher in COAD than in LUAD (p = 0.0182, unpaired t test/two-tailed) (Figure 2c). The C to T mutational signature was significantly higher in COAD than in LUAD (p = 0.0010, unpaired t test/two-tailed) (Figure 2d). APC significantly indirectly co-expressed with MYC in COAD (Figure 2e) but not in LUAD (figure 2f). These results are addressed in the discussion section.
Wnt signaling components SMAD(s) 2/3/4 and TCF7L2 also were found to have increased mutational frequency in COAD over LUAD, each with significant decreased co-expression with MYC (Figure 3a-b).
E2F transcription factors and proliferation subset
E2F dysfunction in cancer has been recently reviewed [40]. E2F4/5/6 are canonical repressors that inhibit target gene expression by complexing with unphosphorylated pocket proteins (RB1, RBL1, and RBL2). Phosphorylation of pocket proteins leads to E2F4 and E2F5 (and E2F3B) removal from the complex, with E2F4/5 shuttled out of the nucleus releasing inhibition or target gene expression.
In this study, E2F4/5/6 co-expression with proliferation factors is deregulated in EGFR-activated tumors (Figure 4a), and an earlier study showed that EGFR activation correlates with decreased expression of proliferation factors [26].
EGFR
LUAD separated into EGFR protein kinase activated versus EGFR nonactivated did not appreciably change the co-expression relationship of EGFR to the proliferation subset (Table 1). While EGFR is overexpressed in COAD, LUAD has most of the activation mutations, many of which are due to exon 19 deletion (Figure 5a-b, Supplemental Figure S1); EGFR is more highly expressed in LUAD (p = 0.0387, unpaired t test/two-tailed) (Figure 5c), and mRNA isoforms exist (Figure 5d). EGFR has a direct ranked co-expression relationship with MYC in COAD and no co-expression relationship in LUAD (Figure 5e-f).
Braf oncogene
Braf activates RAS/MAPK signaling to regulate growth and proliferation; in this study, its expression neither “directly” nor “indirectly” co-expressed with the subset in COAD or the total LUAD cohort. When EGFR-activated cases were removed and assessed on their own, approximately 40% of the proliferation subset had “direct” co-expression with Braf (Table 1) in the remaining non-EGFR LUAD.
Cyclin E:Cdk2/1, Cyclin D:Cdk4/6, and Rb1
Canonical cyclins have periodic expression during the cell cycle, and they complex with specific Cdks controlling their kinase activity. During late G1 and S phase, CCNE1 and Cdk2/1 are highly expressed, and CCND1:Cdk4/6 is reduced. In normal cells when CCND1:Cdk4/6 is expressed, activated, and appropriately distributed subcellularly, it is sensitive to extracellular growth factors and controls progression through G1 and the G1 to S phase transition [41].
In this study, all components of the CCNE1:Cdk2/1 complex directly co-expressed with 94–97% of the genes in the subset in both COAD and LUAD (Supplementary Tables 2–5). Overall alteration in expression and mutation to CCNE1 was 7% in COAD and 5% in LUAD [27–29].
CCND1 had no association with most proliferation factors in COAD or LUAD; overall alteration was 4% in both tumor types. While Cdk4 co-expression ranked directly with a high frequency of proliferative components in both tumor types, CCND1 and Cdk6 did not (Supplemental Tables 2–5).
When LUAD cases were examined as “non-EGFR” versus “EGFR protein kinase activated” cases, CCNE1 directly co-expressed with 97% of the subset in non-EGFR tumors only (Supplemental Table 6).
CCND1:Cdk4/6 proteins physically interact with the retinoblastoma protein, and the resulting phosphorylated complex regulates transcription patterns through E2F factors [42,43]. Rb1 did not have significant co-expression with the subset in COAD (Table 1), and it was mutated or aberrantly expressed in 18% of COAD. Rb1 indirectly co-expressed with a low frequency of the subset in LUAD (Table 1); overall alteration was 16%.
CCNA2:Cdk1/2, CCNA1:Cdk2, CCNB1:Cdk1, and TP53
CCNA2:Cdk1/2 functions in both G1/S transition and down-regulation of G2/M through E2F factor phosphorylation [44–46]. Components of CCNA2:Cdk1/2 co-expressed directly with 94–97% of the subset in both tumor types (Supplemental Tables 2–5).
CCNA1:Cdk2 is associated with the meiotic cell cycle [47–49]; the cyclin co-expressed indirectly with some of the subset in COAD, not in LUAD (Supplemental Tables 2–3).
Multifunctional tumor suppressor TP53 was mutated and/or aberrantly expressed in both COAD (56%) and LUAD (48%), and there was no co-expression association with the proliferation subset in either tumor type (Table 1).
CCNB1:Cdk1 (maturation-promoting factor, MPF) is essential for G2/M transition [50]. Both regulator and kinase directly co-expressed with over 90% of the proliferation gene subset in both tumor types (Supplemental Tables 2–5).
Atypical CCNF
Protein degradation provides an additional level of regulation to the cell cycle; CCNF is part of the Skp1-Cul1-F-box (SCF) family of E3 ubiquitin ligases that controls cell cycle through feedback mechanism affecting E2F1-3, and it is acted upon itself by E2F1, 7/8, and the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/CCdh1) [51].
A slightly reduced frequency of the proliferation subset had direct co-expression association with CCNF in both COAD and LUAD (Supplemental Tables 2 − 3). The genes responsible for the reduction were ORC(s) 2/3/4/5, POLD4, and POLE4, suggesting origin licensing may not be properly regulated by CCNF1:Cdk1-3 in either tumor type.
CCNJ, CCNO:Cdk2, CCNG1:Cdk4/5/6, CCNI:Cdk5
CCNJ knockdown in Drosophila leads to defects in chromosome segregation and progression through mitosis in early embryonic division cycles [52,53]. Complete complexes necessary for origin licensing, firing, and DNA synthesis were not co-expressed fully with CCNJ, in agreement with a role for CCNJ downstream of most of these functions (Supplemental Tables 2–3).
CCNO knockdown is associated with the lung disorder primary dyskinesia [54,55]; it is expressed in multiciliate cells, and it is thought to function in deuterosome-mediated centriole amplification. CCNO:Cdk2 co-expression with the subset was partial in COAD and deregulated with respect to proliferation in LUAD (Supplemental Tables 2–3).
CCNG1 overexpression in yeast leads to inhibition of pre-replicative complexes [56]; reflecting this finding, CCNG1 has indirect co-expression with about two-thirds of the subset in LUAD (Supplemental Tables 2–3). The lack of CCNG1 co-expression with proliferation in COAD has been previously observed [57].
CCNI is an atypical cyclin most abundant in postmitotic cells, and it does not regulate proliferation [58]. Accordingly, CCNI had indirect co-expression with proliferation subset in COAD, and no co-expression correlation in LUAD; Cdk5 ranked directly co-expressed with a moderate frequency of proliferation factors (Supplemental Tables 2–5).
Transcriptional Cdks and their cyclins
Canonical Cdks 1, 2, 4, and 6 are known as “Class I”, and their function is to control cell cycle progression. Transcriptional Cdks (tCdks) 7, 8, 9, 12, 13, 19 make up “Class II”, and they are thought to control pre-initiation complex assembly, initiation, elongation, and spliceosome recruitment in cyclical transcription oscillations [59]. Less well understood functionally, tCdks and their cyclin regulators form complexes CCNH:Cdk7, CCNC:Cdk 8/19 (Mediator complex components), CCNT1:Cdk 9, and CCNK:Cdk 9/12/13.
CCNH:Cdk7, CCNK:Cdk9/12/13, CCNT1:Cdk 9
Cdk7 and Cdk9 are the most studied tCdks at present [59–61]; Cdk7 forms a regulatory complex with CCNH and MNAT1 that has CDK-activating kinase (CAK) activity on Cdk9 and other Cdks and multiple roles in transcription. Cyclin regulator CCNH ranked direct in co-expression with many origin licensing factors in COAD, less in LUAD (Supplemental Tables 2–3); the difference between the two tumor types was significant (p = 0.0106, Fisher’s exact test) (Figure 4b). Cdk7 ranked directly with far fewer genes of the subset in both COAD and LUAD (Supplemental Tables 4–5). CCNT1:Cdk 9 complexes did not uniformly co-express highly with the subset (Supplemental Tables 2–5). These data reflect a “non-cycling” expression pattern of the regulatory cyclins and/or functional roles outside origin licensing, and firing.
CCNK:Cdk12/13 functions by phosphorylating RNA polymerase II C-terminal repeat domain. CCNK:Cdk12 is thought to regulate splicing and 3’-end processing, and knockdown in cell lines inhibits proliferation [62–65]. In accordance with knockdown experiments, CCNK directly co-expressed with some of the proliferation subset in COAD but not in LUAD, suggesting deregulation (Supplemental Tables 2–3); the difference between the two tumor types was significant (p = 0.0079, Fisher’s exact test) (Figure 4b). Cdk12 co-expressed directly with some of the subset in both tumors (Supplemental Tables 4–5). Cdk13 unexpectedly indirectly co-expressed with the proliferation subset in COAD, less so in LUAD (Supplemental Tables 4–5).
Cdk12 protein localizes to the nucleus, where Cdk13 localizes to the nucleus, cytosol, extracellular space, and Golgi apparatus. These observations suggest Cdk13 gets transported out of the nucleus and the plasma membrane; CCNK localizes predominantly to the nucleus [33]. Spearman correlations ranked “indirect” with proliferation factors, and localization of Cdk13 outside of the nucleus suggest Cdk13 may not be involved, or is negatively involved, in proliferation in COAD and LUAD.
CCNC:Cdk 8/19
CCNC and Cdk8 are components of the “Mediator complex”, which bridges transcription factors at promoter DNA, at origin sites, enhancer or silencers, and RNA polymerase; it phosphorylates RNA polymerase II and is required for the expression of all its transcripts [66]. Cdk8 is an oncogene in COAD, and expression knockdown inhibits proliferation [67]. It is overexpressed in 42% of TCGA COAD and acts by increasing transcription of CTNNB1 and MYC, downstream effectors of Wnt signaling [68]. By Spearman correlation, CCNC co-expressed highly with proliferation genes in COAD; however, Cdk8 did not, suggesting Cdk8 overexpression was not solely happening during S phase (Supplemental Tables 2–5). An expression heat map of the proliferation subset in comparison to CCNC and Cdk8 shows cases with Cdk8 overexpression do not have uniformly high or low expression of proliferation factors (Figure 6a). Co-expression of CTNNB1 or MYC is significant and direct with Cdk8 in TCGA PANCAN COAD [67].
CCNC and Cdk8 co-expressed directly with about half of the proliferation subset in LUAD (Supplemental Tables 2–5); the difference in CCNC ranking between COAD and LUAD was significant (p = 0.0486, Fisher’s exact test) (Figure 4b). Overall alteration to the two genes in LUAD is approximately 4–8%.
CCNY:Cdk14
Cdk 14 is highly expressed in brain [69] and interacts with CCND3 and Cdk inhibitor CDKN1A [70]; CDKN1A expression is controlled by TP53 [71]. Cdk14 is associated with Wnt signaling; peak levels of the membrane bound CCNY:Cdk14 complex occur during M phase, not S phase [2]. Accordingly, CCNY had no significant co-expression with the proliferation subset in either COAD or LUAD, and Cdk14 had high indirect co-expression with the subset in COAD (Supplemental Tables 2–5). Overall alteration for both tumor types was 7–8% for CCNY and 9% for Cdk14. CDKN1A Spearman correlation with MYC was examined in COAD and LUAD (Figure 6b), and an indirect relationship was observed for COAD only.
Cdk14 overexpression in relation to proliferation gene co-expression is shown by heat map (Figure 7a). High Cdk14 correlates negatively with proliferation and positively with high hedgehog signaling (HH) and epithelial-to-mesenchyme transition (EMT) markers (Figure 7b); COAD cases with Cdk14 mutation in the protein kinase domain may reverse the correlation, with proliferation co-expression high and HH and EMT low (Figure 7b), Other changes to Wnt signaling when Cdk14 was overexpressed were found for SFRP1/2/4 and DKK1-4 (Figure 7c-d).
Cdk Inhibitors
Cip/kip family, universal inhibitors
CDKN1A, (p21Cip/Waf1) is anti-proliferative, it binds with PCNA and suppresses G1/S and Rb phosphorylation. It is a component of Mediator complex and functions in stem cell maintenance [72–75]. In this study, some indirect correlation with the proliferation subset was seen in COAD (Supplemental Table 7), and co-expression with MYC was indirect (Figure 6b) [27–29]. In LUAD [9,10], significant indirect co-expression was not observed (Supplemental Table 7) nor was indirect co-expression with MYC (Figure 6b), suggesting deregulation.
CDKN1B (p27KIP1) is anti-proliferative; MYC can inactivate the growth arrest it causes [76,77]. In neither tumor type did CDKN1B co-express indirectly with the subset (Supplemental Table 7), nor did CDKN1B co-express indirectly with CCNE1. MYC significantly directly co-expressed with CDKN1B in COAD, not in LUAD [27–29].
CDKN1C (p57KIP2) shares homology with CDKN1A/B and is anti-proliferative causing G1 cell cycle arrest and binding PCNA in S phase, but it singularly functions in embryogenesis [78]. Diverse signals and transcription factors regulate its expression including micro-RNAs and lncRNAs, and imprinting silences it in cancer; its decreased expression is known to be inversely related to tumor growth in both tumor types. In this study, CDKN1C had a high inverse co-expression relationship to the subset in COAD but not LUAD (Supplemental Table 7). Total frequency alteration was 3–6% in COAD and 5–12% in LUAD.
INK4 family, inhibitors of Cdk4/6 and CCND1
CDKN2A isoforms and CDKN2B inhibit Cdk4/6 and stabilize TP53 through MDM2. In COAD, CDKN2A did not co-express with the subset, and CDKN2B indirectly co-expressed (Supplemental Table 7); genetic alterations for both genes were 5–7% of cases, mostly overexpression. In LUAD, CDKN2A unexpectedly directly co-expressed with 26% of the subset. Interestingly, 26% of LUAD had deep deletion or truncation mutations to the gene; mutations likely functionally permit the aberrant direction of co-expression [27–29]. CDKN2B had no co-expression with the subset, consistent with dysregulation; genetic alteration frequency to CDKN2B was 22%, mostly deep deletions.
Both CDKN2C and CDKN2D negatively regulate proliferation, and CDKN2D has its highest transcriptional readout in S phase. In this study, CDKN2C and CDKN2D co-expression with the proliferation subset was deregulated in COAD and LUAD (Supplemental Table 7).
Discussion
Cell cycling depends on coordinated transcriptional oscillations, regulator/effector interactions and subsequent phosphorylation events. Genes responsible for these events are often pharmacological targets in cancer [79]. Spearman’s correlation compares the difference in expression ranking of two genes and identifies the direction of expression relative to each other. The outcomes can be used to follow the transcriptional oscillations of the cell cycle; in this study, they are used to associate genes with DNA synthesis and G1/S phase. Genes used as markers in the proliferation subset have known functions involved in origin licensing, firing, and active DNA synthesis. Methylation, other epigenetic modifications, and the SWI/SNF remodeling complex itself, which play a role in coordinating transcription and proliferation and the definition of origin of replication sites, are not examined.
Among the findings of this investigation, canonical cyclins and the cyclin kinases they regulate co-express with the proliferation subset as expected. For example, CCNE1 responsible for cell cycle G1/S transition co-expresses with the highest frequency of proliferation factors in the subset, as do Cdk(s) 1 and 2. CCNA2:Cdk1/2, driver of proliferation initiation and progression and promoter of mitosis [80], highly co-expresses with the subset as does maturation factor CCNB1. These observations help verify the system used and support findings for genes with less established background.
Wnt signaling
Wnt signaling is fundamental to life. It functions during normal development and cell growth; it becomes aberrantly activated in cancer. The pathway, deduced from the study of multiple models, touches on cell surface events, endocytosis, lysosomal activity, and proteosome degradation, as well as transcriptional events in the nucleus [81,82].
Wnt-based cell cycle signaling peaks during mitosis, as other processes stop [2]. APC controls proliferation through MYC [3], though the mechanism is not fully understood. In vitro MYC over-expression promotes transformation, under-expression decreased proliferation and tumorigenesis, and inactivation promotes mitotic problems, causing apoptosis if the option is available, polyploidy if not. MYC complexes with MAX, MNT, CUBN, and MIZ1, which determine its function [83,84]. It is transcribed during G1 and S phase [85]. Protein domains imply MYC functions in the phosphodegron, chromatin remodeling, and transcription regulation. A MYC-dominant negative mutation will make tumors driven by other genes (e.g. KRAS and TP53) regress, implying MYC regulates large numbers of genes that have never been fully identified. Paradoxically, most of the time, experimental changes to MYC expression do not change mRNA levels of proposed downstream genes; MYC is now thought to control proliferation and tumorigenesis by functioning in basic transcription through the SWI/SNF complex [85] (Figure 1) [14,17–19,21,86–98].
This study shows maximum APC expression happens when MYC availability is at its lowest in COAD. This inverse expression correlates with APC mutation, neither are seen in LUAD. Hypothetically, MYC deregulation in COAD interferes in basic transcription leading to mutation of APC, suggesting that optimum levels, both high and low, at appropriate times during the cell cycle are important for normal Wnt signaling.
The necessity of MYC for proper transcriptional elongation may lend itself particularly to APC where most mutations (often toward the amino terminal of the protein) occur in exon 17, the last exon of the gene. It may also be relevant that COAD has high C to T transitions known to be a transcriptionally associated molecular signature [99], thought as the result of faulty uracil incorporation into DNA. If MYC is not sufficiently around in the absence of TP53, or not completely turned off at the appropriate times to carry out removal of R-loops, for instance, in COAD in Wnt signaling components, conjecturally one could have faulty uracil incorporation leading to the transitions.
Wnt signaling components SMAD(s) 2/3/4 and TCF7L2 also have significant increased mutational frequency in COAD over LUAD, each being expressed with decreased availability of MYC. A second group of Wnt signaling genes (TP53, CSNK2A1, FZD1, and CCND1) are expressed in both COAD and LUAD in a similar MYC (mostly direct) context; their mutational signatures are not significantly different between the two tumor types, lending support to the hypothesis.
Universal Cdk inhibitor CDKN1A (p21 Cip/Waf1), whose expression is normally turned off by MYC and whose protein competes with MYC for a PCNA binding site, also did not indirectly co-express with MYC in LUAD as it does in COAD, supporting deregulation of MYC expression in LUAD. CDKN1A does significantly indirectly rank with Braf in LUAD, and Braf direct co-expression with proliferation factors was found elevated in non-EGFR-activated LUAD. In normal lung and colon, MYC/MYCL/MYCN and KRAS expression are comparable; the fact that MYC co-expression with proliferation factors does not rank directly with high frequency suggests that MYC expression is deregulated with respect to S phase in LUAD.
MAPK signaling
Unlike Wnt signaling where multiple fields of research suggested several cellular processes engaged in the same pathway, MAPK (mitogen activated protein kinase pathway) was identified as a family of protein-serine/threonine kinases activated in response to a variety of hormones and growth factors signaling to affect proliferation. MYC is a target gene of both Wnt and MAPK signaling. MYC and KRAS involvement in cancer is thought to be co-operative and contextual genetically, and how they co-operate is not fully understood; their role in the immune response and STAT signaling is under investigation [39]. KRAS deregulation in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has recently been linked to cytokines usage from the tumor microenvironment [100], providing candidate therapeutic targets in the activated KRAS pathway in this tumor type.
In this study, KRAS and MYC co-expressed directly with a high frequency of proliferation genes in COAD but not LUAD. The difference implies an alteration in the mechanism by which MAPK signaling is regulated. Interestingly, both genes are mutated roughly to the same extent in both tumor types, and the changes are highly comparable (Figure 8a-b). Although high expressors exist, MYC amplification does not generally lead to increased transcription in either tumor type.
EGF is a mitogen that can trigger both MAPK and Wnt signaling upon coupling with its receptor, EGFR. EGFR activation mutation by exon nineteen deletion is found in LUAD, not COAD. In COAD, EGFR has a direct co-expression relationship with MYC, and EGFR mutations are not found. More highly expressed in LUAD, EGFR has no significant direct ranked co-expression with MYC (Figure 5e-f), and mutations are found. Interestingly, cases with mutations are located predominantly above the EGFR/MYC Spearman correlation curve (figure 5f, and Supplementary Figure S1A), suggesting higher EGFR transcription in those cases in lower MYC context. This is not identifiable, examining median mRNA expression levels. In LUAD, EGFR does not significantly co-express directly with CCNK, which might imply splicing issues that could lead to the exon nineteen deletion.
Cell cycle
Progression from G1 into S phase occurs when retinoblastoma (Rb) is inactivated by phosphorylation, releasing E2F transcription factors. The relationship of E2F(s) (1–8) with proliferation was examined to suggest Rb1 phosphorylation status a priori, as phosphorylation data for individual cases was not available. In LUAD, Rb1 alteration was mostly due to under expression, implying Rb1 was both inactivated and under expressed. E2F(s) (1–8) co-expression ranked directly with a high frequency of proliferation factors, and mostly indirectly with Rb1 itself.
In EGFR-activated LUAD, E2F(s)4/5/6 expression was completely deregulated with respect to S phase. E2Fs 4/5 normally function as repressors and are under Rb control, and as it is inactivated by phosphorylation, they get shuttled out of the nucleus as complexes are disrupted [40]. Knockdown experiments have suggested that E2F6 controls progression through S phase, as S phase length is shortened [101]. However, E2F(s)4/5/6 were not mutated or aberrantly expressed (above or below the diploid tumor fraction), and this type of evidence was not found to confirm S phase timing alteration. Collectively, the data suggest that EGFR protein kinase activation competes with Cyclin/Cdk complexes, leading to inappropriate phosphorylation of RB1, RBL1, and RBL2 that prevents release of E2F(s)4/5 and subsequent cytoplasmic localization and proliferation. In a normal cell, cyclin D:Cdk4/6, responsive to extracellular signals such as EGF, is thought to monophosphorylate Rb1 in early G1 at 14 different sites, which lead to preferential E2F binding patterns [43]. EGFR-activated protein kinase probably interferes with this process, as well as having the potential to phosphorylate other substrates.
Another interesting consequence of removing EGFR-activated cases from the LUAD cohort is the subsequent rise in the frequency of Braf direct ranked co-expression with genes of the proliferation subset. Mathematical removal of EGFR cases is a bit analogous to treating clinically with specific EGFR inhibitors, eliminating EGFR-activated cells from tumor heterogeneity. The data suggest in many remaining cases that Braf is more co-expressed with proliferation genes, at the same time, KRAS and MYC become more deregulated with respect to S phase. Recent reports of a connection between Braf and EGFR-acquired resistance mutations have been seen in several tumor types [102,103]. Taken as a model, removal of cases with specific driver mutations and examination of the proliferation potential of remaining cases may be useful in identifying potential drivers of resistance where anti-tumor reagents exist; the fact that EGFR and Braf are both members of the same signaling pathway (MAPK) may be significant. It may also suggest that synthetic lethality could be achieved by simultaneous use of inhibitors to both EGFR and Braf, if tolerable for the patient [104].
E2F(s)1–8 also co-expressed highly with proliferation factors in total COAD; however, in this tumor type, Rb1 was mostly over expressed. E2F(s) 3,5,6,7, and 8 all significantly directly co-expressed with Rb1 itself, implying release by Rb1 inactivation. Rb1, CCND1, and Cdk6 appeared deregulated with respect to proliferation in COAD.
CCNY:Cdk14
Cell cycling is distinguished from the quiescence phase (G0) observed in most stem cells by stages G1, S, G2, and M. G0 is defined as absence of proliferation with maintenance of proliferative potential [42]. Growth factors control progression from G0 to G1, and S phase is marked by a restriction point after which growth factors have no effect. When examining CCNY:Cdk14, a membrane complex linked to Wnt signaling whose peak expression is thought during M phase [2,105–107], and Cdk14 overexpression without its CCNY regulator was found to correspond indirectly with proliferation gene expression and directly with co-expression of hedgehog signaling and epithelial-to-mesenchyme transition (EMT) genes in COAD and most LUAD. The few COAD with Cdk14 mutations appeared to reverse the heat map expression patterns for proliferation, hedgehog signaling, and EMT components. This behavior is reminiscent of the binary switch between G0 and proliferation; some evidence points to Cdk14 function in patterning and cell proliferation during embryonic development [108]; regulator CCNY was identified by yeast two-hybrid screen [106]. Cigarette smoking may decrease Cdk14 levels in LUAD [109]. LUAD had more cases with high CCNY expression, suggesting a mechanism for Wnt signaling activation in this proportion of the tumor type.
Transcriptional cyclins and tCDKs
CCNC, CCNH, and CCNK are “non-cycling” cyclin regulators of tCdks, which generally explains their lack of a uniformly high direct rank co-expression with S phase proliferation factors. However, they do correlate with the decrease in direct rank co-expression with the proliferation subset between COAD and LUAD (Figure 7b). MYC, KRAS, CCNC, CCNH, and CCNK all have significant decreased frequency of direct ranked co-expression with essential proliferation factors in LUAD when compared to COAD. Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription complex includes, among other proteins, CCNC: Cdk8/19 and Med12/13. CCNC co-expression ranked directly with a high frequency of proliferation genes in COAD, less in LUAD; unexpectedly, Cdk8 was not highly correlated with proliferation in COAD. Since Cdk8 overexpression occurs in about half of all COAD, it is thought of as an oncogene [67]. The present study indicates Cdk8 over-expression is not during S phase alone in COAD and that not all cases with high Cdk8 expression necessarily have high proliferative potential.
Summary
In COAD, maximum APC expression happens when MYC availability is at its lowest, and a high majority of cases have APC mutation. Neither inverse co-expression with MYC nor mutation of APC are seen in LUAD. APC is more highly transcribed in COAD than LUAD having a high C-to-T transition rate, a signature often associated with transcriptional mutation. MYC is thought to play a role in R loop persistence through the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex. Many COAD have APC mutated in the context of TP53 mutation, making senescence impossible and cellular immortality likely in the case of MYC inactivation. Alternatively, as some COAD with APC mutation do not have TP53 mutation, it may be that MYC is not completely turned off at M phase, leading to persistent R loops causative of APC truncation.
